subsubtopic: ALLEGED THREATS AGAINST THOSE WHO WORK ON OCTOBER 14TH-REQUEST FOR ACTION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to propose a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43, and I hope 1 will get support from both sides of the House for my motion. Literally hundreds of union members, even their spouses and children, have come to my constituency office or telephoned or written to me to tell me of threats against their livehoods and even their families if they work on October 14. They tell of losing their democratic freedoms within our free democracy.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser):
That the relevant departments and agencies of government undertake an immediate investigation to determine the extent and degree of intimidation used to prevent rank and file trade unionists from working on October 14, 1976, and to identify any individuals who should be prosecuted for the use of threats of violence or other reprisals to prevent any person from working, and to prepare legislation to assure every trade unionist of the right to determine their own economic destinies through supervised free and secret ballot at all times.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO DEAL WITH IMPORTATION OF MEAT- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the recent beef embargo imposed by President Ford of the United States, and in view of the fact that the Canadian beef industry has been in a serious depression for a considerable period of time, more particularly in the last few months, and in view of Canada's sellout in respect of the Canada-Australia-New Zealand meat agreement, and, further, that because of the United States embargo the Canadian beef industry faces the very real possibility of even heavier volumes of beef from Australia and New Zealand, no doubt already in transit to the United States market, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave):
That the Minister of Agriculture take immediate action to ensure that this product will not be dumped on our Canadian market and to place immediately, if necessary, a temporary embargo on beef from Australia and New Zealand and, secondly, that the minister implement a long overdue Canadian meat import law, and, finally, that he negotiate with his United States counterparts a longer term agreement having regard for historical trade patterns.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have pointed out to the former minister of national defence, and I remind the Leader of the Opposition of this, that last March I wrote to the premiers and gave them three options whereby we thought we could patriate the constitution. Only

one of them referred to language rights and an entrenched amending formula; at least one of the other two, as I recall, contained nothing on language rights. This is a government whose period in office is measured not by elections or by parliaments but by advertising slogans. I was interested to read reports of the Prime Minister's speech in Toronto the other day. That was his speech to the faithful; at least, there were some faithful reported to be there when it began. In that speech the Prime Minister lamented the state of the nation. He even lamented the state of the Liberal

party. Well, Mr. Speaker, my lament is not for Canada; I have sufficient confidence in the strength of the people of this country to believe that they can survive even this government.

I must say that, difficult though it is, I am able to restrain my sorrow for the state of the Liberal party. My lament instead, Sir, is for a Prime Minister and for a government that have become so isolated, so divorced from reality, that they cannot even hear let alone respond to the message of Canadians. My lament is that we have to suffer through this total lack of leadership for another two years until the Prime Minister gives the people of Canada a chance to make a fresh start.
I found, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure many other Canadians did, a particular significance in the words "operation justification". Because that indicates that this government does not believe that there is anything wrong with the substance of its policies. Its members are prepared to go out and not question those policies to justify them. They believe the only problem is with the perception of those policies. In other words, it is not the government that is at fault, it is the people of Canada who are at fault.
There is no intention evidenced, either in the outpourings in Toronto or in the carefully empty speech of yesterday, of any change in the substance of the policies; the government is merely trying to cajole Canadians to change the nature of their response to policies that are clearly inadequate to the requirements of modern Canada. There is no program. There are simply to be public relations on the part of the government in the remaining months of its mandate, and unfortunately that emphasis on public relations began in the throne speech that we received yesterday.

The end is a free society of men and women and children . . . and free collective bargaining and the free enterprise system are some tools we have devised to reach that goal. Against that position were raised equally strong voices supporting the private sector, as in this statement:
Our strongest and most promising asset is the spirit of the people of Canada, our willingness to tackle difficult challenges head-on, our tradition of self-reliance, responsibility and individual intiative.

But, if this throne speech was to have any relevance in current Canadian reality, it had to include above all some sense of direction for Canada, some idea of what the government really intends to do with the current controls program and, equally important, what goals it has for the country as we emerge from that program. Canadians do not know where the government is leading them. The Prime Minister and his colleagues have piled conflicting statement on conflicting statement to the point where the overwhelming characteristic of the Canadian mood is sheer uncertainty.
The government had the opportunity, and I believe the obligation in this throne speech, at least to begin the process of easing that uncertainty; of at least beginning to come clean with Canadians. Instead of that we are given some vague talk about the "middle road", and even more vague promises to begin-note, "to begin"-a process of consultation.
What a confession that is for a government to make; that after a full 12 months of controls it is now thinking seriously of beginning a consultative process. It was clear when this program was first proposed here that the purpose of bringing in controls was to buy some time, to get some breathing space that would allow that kind of consultation, and that would allow the bringing together of the economic partners of Canada in order that we might get some agreement as to what we were going to do once the controls' period was ended.
Having it clearly understood that that was the purpose of the program the government stole, why did it take the government 12 months and even more to begin the simple process of consultation? This was the government that boasted it had its full contingency plans ready some three years ago. Instead of contingency plans and instead of consultation we have wasted a full year, a year in which we have not only begun to suffer the inevitable distortions of a controls regime, but during which the climate for securing some kind of consensus of agreement among the partners in the economy has been seriously eroded, thanks to the Prime Minister's propensity for loose talk and confrontation politics.

In reading it, no one can detect the fact that Canada is facing a serious problem of balance of payments and that its

competitive position on international markets is continually eroding.

The government asserts its concern about inflation, yet nowhere does it acknowledge that it controls the most basic price of all, the price of money, and that interest rates in this country remain at extremely high inflationary levels. Indeed, we are treated in the name of a housing policy to a rerun of that old cliche about one million starts every four years, when anyone who has cared enough to talk to young Canadian families knows that the main problem today is not finding a house, but is finding the money to finance a mortgage.

It is not unusual for a throne speech to be obscure or imprecise, but this speech is much more than that. This speech is misleading. It uses soothing words to try to deny the direction in which the government has been carrying the country. It praises consultation when the government's consistent position has been to act unilaterally. It talks about "a reliance on the market to stimulate growth" when this government, through delays and threats and constant changes, has done more than any other agency to inhibit that kind of growth.
It talks about reducing the number of public servants and is silent about the increasing number of consultants the govern-

ment has acquired, often without the protection and the standards guaranteed by the Public Service Commission.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is bad enough that a government in mid-mandate, elected with a solid majority, should use a throne speech to mislead instead of lead. But that is particularly damaging for this government because Canadians have come to expect that this is a government which cannot be believed. Its history has been marked not simply by changes but by absolute reversals.
In 1974 the Prime Minister campaigned against the very idea of controls. We can remember him pointing his finger on the television screen saying, "zap, you are frozen", and then a year later he imposed what he had opposed. On May 10 he told the trilateral commission that, "to me that is the end of separatism"; and ten days ago in Toronto he said, "But now, perhaps, an increasing number of French Canadians think they do have somewhere to go. And there is a legal political party which for a variety of reasons is getting a large percentage of the vote in Quebec."
This throne speech tip-toes toward greater freedom of information; yet the government still hides the secret reports on post controls prepared by the ten deputy ministers, the group known as the DM ten. The speech again says controls will come off, but then it goes on to propose to negotiate their extension with the provinces. In all of this there is one clear message, which is that no amount of flim-flam can obscure the fact that this is a government that Canadians cannot trust.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And without trust it is a government that cannot govern, because a basis of trust in a federal and diverse country like Canada is elemental to national unity.
I want to speak for a moment about national unity because I think there has been a mistake in assuming that bilingualism, important as that is, is the only implement or the only issue of national unity in Canada.

Due to the agreement given by all parties in this House, bilingualism has become law and it will remain a basic principle of any Progressive Conservative government which is assured of receiving then as it does now the support of the minority parties in this House. However, the manner in which bilingualism has been implemented has caused some concern among many Canadians, French-speaking as well as Englishspeaking, but there is no reason to call them bigots or racists. On the contrary, what they need is to consider calmly various injustices now existing in the public service or elsewhere so that the program will be efficient in terms of the law and will be accepted in practice. This is our party's commitment. [English]
Constitutions are important; laws are important. But this country is more than laws, more than constitutions; it is above all a partnership, and the essence of partnership in this country

is to establish a basis of mutual respect and trust. That has broken down in Canada. It is not an accident that it has broken down. It is not due to impersonal forces from abroad. It has broken down because of now nearly a decade of the practice by this government of taking unpredicted unilateral actions and unilateral decisions to withdraw from shared costs programs which previously were forced upon the provinces, of unilateral changes in the anti-inflation board controls after many of the people affected by those controls had just gone through the costly process of adjusting to the rules that had been there, and of unilateral imposition of the program of controls without any consultation with the Canadian Labour Congress or any of the other partners who were directly to be affected.
You cannot run a country unilaterally. You cannot run it on your own. The mistake the government has made, and which it seems intent on continuing to make, is that it alone is the government which can call all the shots in Canada. Of course we need in this nation a strong national government, but we also need in this nation strong provincial governments, a strong private sector, a strong labour movement, a strong agriculture, and a number of other partners who can work together to achieve the promise and the potential of this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

What we have instead is an administration that is governed by surprise-changing the AIB regulations without warning, bringing in controls without warning, and depriving Canadians of the climate of certainty which they need to plan their own lives and to pursue their own goals free of the fear that the rules will change in the middle of the night. [Translation]
The Speech from the Throne briefly referred to the formal constitutional independence of our country. I am sure all hon. members would agree to the patriation of the constitution. However, we must not forget that we are now dealing with two issues. One is purely symbolic: It is bringing back home the document; the other is essential: It implies an agreement on the amendment formula which would make the constitution workable. At a time when the provinces do not trust the federal government disagreement over the amendment formula is to be expected. We should all be aware of the danger that the relentless pursuit of the symbol may jeopardize the chances of an agreement about the amendment formula.
There appears to be some question about the accuracy or the nature of the interpretation of the stance of the Government of Canada on the constitutional questions by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson), the former minister of national defence. I presume that there were also other reasons for his resignation. I want to put that question aside, however, regarding the apparent reason for his resignation because one of the things that is most significant about the resignation which occurred this morning is that the hon. member for

Winnipeg South, who did not have to come to parliament for a career, was one of many Canadians in 1968 who thought the present Prime Minister would bring a fresh and hopeful spirit to national affairs. 1 do not know if the former minister of national defence feels deceived; I do know he feels disappointed, and for the country the tragedy is not that one more minister has gone; it is that the Prime Minister who was the repository of so much hope was prepared to trade it all away to take the advice of his flim-flam friends who contrive different incarnations whenever public opinion polls change.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

There is plenty of rhetoric in this speech about the potential greatness of Canada. We all know about that potential and we all accept it, but the job of government, the challenge of the real leadership, is not simply to tell us about our potential; it is to help guide the country toward responding to that potential.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

This government is in an unique position to do that. It has a solid majority in parliament although it is beginning to show strains and, until tomorrow's news at least, it has a full two years remaining in its present mandate. guarantee of that reality, that if controls come off, suddenly there will be no increase in the inflation rate.

It is evident that Canadians know they have benefitted under controls, and will benefit still further as the program continues to restrain prices and protect real income gains next year and into 1978. At the outset of the program, we said the immediate target was an inflation rate of 8 per cent by the end of the first year of the program. We are meeting this target. Our success so far gives us confidence that we will also meet next year's more difficult target of 6 per cent.
As we enter the second year of the program, Canadians can expect a further reduction in the rate of wage increases, a further reduction in the rate of price increases, a further reduction in the rate of increase of government spending and the growth of the public service.
And as those reductions take effect, we will approach closer to one of the major longer-term objectives of the anti-inflation program-a more realistic level of expectations among Canadians in relation to future income and price increases.
To accelerate the movement toward more realistic expectations, and to lay the groundwork for the removal of controls without a renewal of inflation, the government will be asking Canadians to take part in the consideration of economic and social policies appropriate to balanced growth without controls, and without inflation.

That is why the government over the coming months will seek the close co-operation of Parliament, the provincial governments, business, labour and the general public in focussing on the priority problems the government has identified, on the strategies we will propose, and on choosing from among the options which we will define.
Those choices, and their co-operative adoption by Canadians, are the second crucial element in the anti-inflation program. Controls buy us the time to make the changes necessary for future stability and growth. The government has been using the time provided by the first year of controls to analyze the major economic problems which lie in the path of our future stability, and to define the options available to us. Now it is time for the second phase of that process, the involvement of Canadians generally in making the important choices presented to us by the difficult and promising times in which we live. As those choices are made, they will be translated into new laws and new working mechanisms for achieving growth without inflation.
In the consultation process which will be an integral part of both the further refinement of price and income controls, and the development of new strategies, the government will be very responsive to the concerns and ideas of the people it serves, but will not swerve from its determination to remove inflation as the major threat to our economic health. The strategic areas upon which we hope to focus the attention and action of Canadians are employment policies, social policies, labour-management relations, the sharing of social responsibility, decentralization, growth and investment.
It will quickly become apparent, to all who choose to join with us in tackling the present impediments to stable growth, that inflation is a pervasive disease that is as serious a social and cultural problem as it is an economic one. It is because of the government's commitment to Liberal social goals that we place a particularly high priority upon dampening those inflationary forces which impede full employment, greater mutual respect, safety and health in the working place, and the decentralization of economic opportunities.
We invite the working men and women of Canada to be full partners in the pursuit of social justice and equality of opportunity, to join us under the umbrella of the law of the land in choosing better ways toward a better future for all Canadians.

Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, when I was asked for a quick response to the throne speech I said that it had obviously been ghost-written by Dr. Gallup and that political expediency virtually oozed from each of its paragraphs. After an evening of reflection and spending some several hours in preparation for today's debate, and after listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) this afternoon, I feel my comments of last night were indeed a model of restraint.
The throne speech is a political document. It is punctuated throughout with the cynicism that underlines the government's contempt for the people of our country. I say contempt most

seriously, because in more than two years since the last election the Liberal party has done nothing to deal with the problems it said were pressing in 1974. Now, having reached an all-time low in popularity, it thinks Canadians can be bought off with glib phrases.
Nowhere in the throne speech does the government indicate that it is planning a massive response to the worst level of unemployment in modern times. Instead the government responds with rhetoric which might improve its standing in the popularity polls.
Nowhere in the speech does the government indicate it has a policy to deal with the crisis of rising oil and gas prices. Instead it only talks of an awareness of the need for conservation of energy resources.
Nowhere in the Speech from the Throne does the government indicate it is prepared to come to grips with the serious housing needs of the people of Canada. Instead it complacently admits that its currently inadequate housing policies will have to do in the future.
The outline of the government's proposals reads like a litany of past and future evasions. In almost every case the government touches on some important element of Canadian life only to avoid coming to grips with the issues. And, as I have already said, the Speech makes no more than a passing reference to three of our most serious problems-jobs, energy, and housing. When the federal government, the senior level of government, can produce a document as cynical as that which was read from the Throne yesterday, is it any wonder so many people today are turned off by politics and politicians?
Why should Canadians take their government or politicians seriously when the governing politicians ignore the real problems facing the vast majority of the people? Why should they trust the government, particularly the government of the present Prime Minister, a politician who in 1974 campaigned for office pledging action in specific areas and totally rejecting wage and price controls? What we got were controls and no action on the specific problems which were the subject of his undertakings. Mr. Speaker, no politician in this country has done more than the present Prime Minister to foster the skepticism with which Canadians increasingly view political activities.
Canadians are fed up with political promises of a "just society", or more recently a "new society", when those promises come from a party which vacillates instead of leading. Now, according to the Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister has embarked upon a program to build a "middle society", a society in which "individual initiative" and "reliance on the market" become the touchstones of government policy, a so-called "middle society" where social goals are pursued by improving the market because that is what the business community wants.
Does the Prime Minister think Canadians cannot see through this middle-of-the-road nonsense? Does the government think Canadians will not recognize this cynicism?
October 13, 1976

Achieving social justice and equality of opportunity in our society demands a commitment to change existing structures which have remained unjust and unequal for too long. Yet here we find the government stating categorically that it has no intention of attempting any change which might offend the established order. The message from Bay Street during the summer of '76 has gotten through to the Prime Minister's office.
The real significance of the Speech from the Throne is that it stands as a Liberal party policy paper revealing the disorganized and impoverished state of its authors. It shows clearly that this besieged gaggle has consciously returned to Mackenzie King cynicism. The Liberal message from now on will be, "We are finished with openly trying to build a better society." Liberals will stand instead for the "middle way", the way that carries no commitment. Well, the middle way is really the muddled way, and Canadians know it. It is a way which enables cynical politicians to try to have it both ways. However, the people know better now than to fall for that kind of game.
The Speech from the Throne may or may not have been the swan song of the Prime Minister-we shall have to wait a few more months to see whether his party can survive with him- but it unquestionably laid to rest his political credibility. This latest flip-flop, this calculated muddling, won't wash with Canadians. It comes too close on the heels of the broken promise concerning wage and price controls. It comes at a time when Canadians want leadership and commitment in coming to grips with their problems, not glib responses to popularity polls. It comes also at a time when Canadians can see the Official Opposition party busy providing no alternative. Canadians witness not only Liberal cynicism but also Tory opportunism.
If the audience is the Chamber of Commerce, the Tory position is that profits must be uncontrolled. If the audience contains a sprinkling of trade unionists the Tories claim to understand why workers wish to protest against controls. One day the Conservatives take credit for wage controls, and the next they condemn those controls. The ghost of Mackenzie King is schizophrenic; not content with the Prime Minister's residence, it has also taken up residence in Stornoway.
The Canadian public looks to the official opposition for an alternative. Instead they find the same calculated vacillations as those of which the government is guilty. The voter looks to the Tories for unity of purpose, and finds instead a continuation of disunity. Canadians fed up with Liberal flip-flops will soon see that Conservative indecision is not one whit better. The Tories say they are keeping their programs secret until the election; no doubt they are, because were they to be revealed now they would be seen to be as vacuous as yesterday's throne speech.
This second session of the thirtieth parliament could, if the Prime Minister and the government chose, go a long way toward reducing the skepticism felt by the average person toward government and politics. What is required is a readiness to come to grips with the real issues. The official opposi-
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
tion, too, could help overcome this skepticism if Conservatives were prepared to question intelligently and offer honest, identifiable alternative approaches to issues which concern the average Canadian.
In short, Canadians want an end to cynicism. They don't expect magic but they do w.ant action. They are tired of phony debate on constitutional crises created whenever the Liberals find themselves in political difficulty. They want our constitution brought home to Canada where it can quickly be brought up to date so that the whole country can deal with more pressing issues.
Canadians are tired-and I say this with emphasis-of the bungling on bilingualism. They are prepared to build a bilingual Canada, but both French and English speaking Canadians want fair programs that are explained to them. They are tired of being lectured at and resent being told that every criticism of the present program is a challenge to the very principle of bilingualism. They are tired, in short, of that phony argument.
Working Canadians are tired of government inaction on industrial and environmental health and safety problems. They know what and where the hazards to health and safety are. They know precisely the corporations that are causing these problems and what immediate, straightforward, practical steps would have to be taken to clear them up.
The miners whom I talked to not long ago at Elliot Lake know just what dangers they face from lung cancer, from white-hand or silicosis. They know that unless ventilation is improved when production is expanded conditions will be as hazardous as before. They know it is critically dangerous not to wear uncomfortable and inefficient masks-something as mundane but as serious as that. What they want to know is why the federal government, which has responsibility for uranium development, does not share the responsibility of paying for the research needed to eliminate the long-term effects of mine-related diseases. Why, they ask, has the federal government failed even to help develop a safe mask which the private sector refuses to produce for its workers in the mines?
Canadians also want to know why regulations governing leeching from radioactive tailings threaten their drinking water at home and have made unsafe the water that the local Indian band in the neighbourhood has to drink. The Cree of Cross Lake, whom I visited this fall in Manitoba, want to know why it took six years to get federal action in obtaining safe drinking water.
I was shocked and moved, Mr. Speaker, when I discovered in September that in August of 1976-I repeat, August of 1976-92 Indian kids had been seriously affected with diarrhoea and gastroenteritis and nothing had been done. I am pleased to report that at least the new Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) promptly initiated corrective action when I drew his attention to the problem, but surely, Mr. Speaker, his department and his predecessors stand condemned for decades of past inaction toward our native people.

The Address-Mr. Broadbent

They are tired of a federal government that is incapable of preparing a competent energy policy for the whole country. Atlantic Canadians, and I think particularly of Canadians in the provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island who for years have been ignored by the absence of an effective regional development program, want to know why they must suffer again disproportionately in this energy crisis.

Here more than anywhere else in federal policy do we find our people calling for serious reform. The average working Canadian family is overtaxed or taxed unfairly, and wants relief. They do not want to avoid their burden but they do want a fair burden. They know that corporations do not pay their fair share of the tax bill. They know, for example, that in 1970 corporations paid a higher proportion of federal taxes than they do today in 1976, after so many years of so-called progressive government.
Most taxpayers recall with dismay the fact that our former leader, David Lewis, revealed in the 1972 election campaign that corporations had amassed tax deferrals of some $4.8 billion that they would never have to repay. The important thing to remember here is that these are interest free loans to corporations that no Canadian, if he wants to buy a house, can get from his government. But a corporation with its connections with the Liberal party can get billions of dollars in deferred taxes. My party described that situation in 1972 as a corporate rip-off. It remains unchanged. In 1976 it remains a corporate rip-off.
However, Mr. Speaker, the government, with the active encouragement of the Conservatives, has solved the problem for at least one group of taxpayers. It has created a whole new batch of personal tax gimmicks so that the wealthy at least can enjoy their own private rip-off. The Government calls the corporate tax dodges investment incentives. The personal tax dodges are called, both by the government and by the official opposition, saving incentives. Technically every Canadian is eligible for these new tax dodges. In reality only the well-off can afford to take advantage of registered retirement savings plans, registered home ownership plans, dividend tax credits, $1,000 interest income deductions, or half tax rates on capital gains.
The unfair distortion created by these so-called incentives comes very clearly into focus when Revenue Canada can report in 1974 that 252 people who made more than $50,000 paid no income taxes at all. Under this government's tax proposals, many of which were first suggested by the official opposition, there were 252 people earning more than $50,000 a year who paid not one cent in income tax. In 1973 the number was 156, and in 1972 the number was 92. The point I am making is that the situation has been getting regressively worse numerically.
What was the average income of this poor group that paid no taxes? The average income was $92,000 a year. That was the average of those who paid no taxes. Had they paid taxes at the rate of 40 per cent the federal treasury would have been richer by $10 million, and something useful might have been done with that money. The precise point is that this money could have been used in the way of equity to reduce the burden on the other people. Instead, because we have this kind of loophole for the rich, every other Canadian has had to subsidize these 252.
Let me stress that the money involved would not amount to very much of a savings for the other taxpayers. 1 think it works out to about $1 each, but that is not the point. The issue is one of fairness in the tax system. We do not have a fair tax system when Canadians earning $92,000 a year pay no taxes at all while other men and women whose family incomes are at the poverty level have to pay taxes. That is the situation we have under this Liberal government. Taxes were not even mentioned in yesterday's throne speech.
Let me now return to the redistribution of income, and I was astounded to read one argument. It was absurdly stated that the redistribution of income has been "obstructed by inflation". I was further astounded by the statement that "to support private industry in meeting greater international com-

The Prime Minister is right. Of course they are better off. They are better off by .5 per cent. All I can say is that that is slim pickings for Canada's poor. The point obviously is that if the government had been concerned about that precise group, the unorganized workers, it could have done what the labour party did in Great Britain when it brought in a very different kind of controls program and made certain levels of increases mandatory for the poor people. That was precisely what the Liberals left out in this country.
I do not care what the Prime Minister or other officials say, price increases in this country remain essentially and virtually uncontrolled. Despite spending $1 million in taxes on a misleading advertising campaign, the controls program has not been the cause of the reduction in the rate of increase in the consumer price index. The government claims credit for the weather which has resulted in better crops and lower interna-

tional food prices. At home meat prices in particular have fallen at the farm gate. Yes, indeed, some of those declines in food prices at the farm gate have been passed on, but I repeat that food prices are virtually uncontrolled, and the main reason we are receiving benefits now as consumers of food is the work done by the Canadian farmers at home and by other farmers abroad, and not the controls program. When you subtract the food component from the consumer price index, what do we find? We find that we have an actual rate of inflation of about 9.3 per cent and that we have a rate of inflation still in housing in the neighbourhood of 13.5 per cent.
Earlier today the Prime Minister had questions concerning where we stood in respect of profits. I reply to the Prime Minister that of course we support the notion that if we have a private sector there will be profits. That was not the argument. The argument I made outside the Elouse in speeches to which he was alluding is that if you are to control profits at all then you set the same kind of restrictions and limitations on them that you set on the ordinary wage and salary earnings, and if you have a $2,400 ceiling, or a 2 per cent maximum on productivity gains for workers, why in heavens name do we not have the same kind of ceiling on profits for the corporate sector? That is the argument.
In the list of speeches 1 made prior to the opening of the House I provided the names of all kinds of corporations, somewhere between 55 and 60, whose profits are up 25 per cent over last year, 50 per cent, 75 per cent, and indeed over 100 per cent. I referred to these cases, and not one fact has been challenged. I wish publicly to give credit to the research group of the New Democratic Party which did the work on that project. I want to say to the Prime Minister that it is a very unfair program when Simpsons-Sears can increase its profits in that kind of range, or when Canadian Tire can go up 25 per cent or 30 per cent, whatever the figure is.
The argument has been made that their sales have been increasing. I think the Prime Minister asked this afternoon whether that does not entail their right to have more profits. I say that our version of a just controls program is that it does not entail that right; that if their sales are increasing in such a way that their profits are going up 25 per cent, 50 per cent or 80 per cent, then instead of having a system which permits them to go up we should have a system which compels them to reduce their prices and pass on the benefits to the consumers. That is what the program should be all about.
I want to conclude my remarks by saying that the controls program that has been brought in-and we said this all along, not in some empty-handed kind of way which made no distinction at all about the right of corporations to have profits, which of course they must have-is unfair to working Canadians. The evidence supports this because their wages and salaries have been held down while at the same time profits have not been held in check in the private sector.
To speak of a third element in the population, we have the executive salaries which have been permitted to go up because of stock options and because of income received from dividends in an unchecked way. Also there is the situation in

petition, the government will modify substantial industrial assistance programs". This boggles the mind. Here we have a government controlling wages of workers; a government which has failed even to begin the redistribution of income in this country; a government which says it will practise restraint, yet a government that is going to increase substantially once again give-away programs to private industry.
What Canadians want to know is how much we have to pay in taxes to keep enterprise free and initiative stimulated. They are sick of paying unfair taxes. A few years ago we were told we needed all these tax write-offs, tax deferrals, and industrial assistance programs to create jobs. Today we have more unemployed Canadians than at any other time in modern history. Even a finance department study, and 1 emphasize that, which was agreed to under conditions of a minority government, and which reported back a couple of years ago, concluded that these give-aways amounting to billions of dollars each year to the corporations were simply not working and not achieving the numbers of jobs they were designed to create. Yet we still have the same programs on the books, and in the throne speech we were informed that they are to be made even more bountiful for the corporations, and this is at a time, as I say, when those at the poverty level continue to pay taxes, and at a time when individuals earning $92,000 a year pay no taxes. This boggles the mind, particularly when we have this new kind of commitment to corporate give-aways.
At the same time the government is callously cutting off the unemployed from the benefits they need because the jobs we paid for in our tax system last year have not been created. The more than 700,000 Canadians listed as unemployed want work, not handouts. There is a phrase almost like that in the throne speech, but the phrase is not followed up by any commitment to action.
This government simply tinkers with unemployment programs that do little more than extend inefficient and inadequate existing programs. The money the government will spend is the money it will have saved by cutting off the benefits of those already without jobs. That is remarkable logic. You take away from the poor and unemployed and use that same money to provide them with benefits. Instead of going to those who are more adequately situated financially, and instead of doing some serious economic planning involving the private sector, the government takes the money from the poor to provide for the poor. This is the worst kind of political cynicism.
The people of Canada want a government commitment to full employment policies, and policies that will result in at least $7 billion in additional national production, which is currently being lost as a result of current levels of unemployment.
The people want a commitment to housing policies which hold out hope for reasonable rental accommodation and reasonable home ownership costs. We want an end to mortgage rates of 11.75 per cent. A direct solution simply involves direct and tough action with our financial institutions. We want people in Toronto and other cities to be able to look at
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
houses which cost less than $68,776. We want them to be able to look at row condominiums which cost less than $50,204, which is the typical price, and at a cost less than $41,175, the current price of an apartment condominium in Toronto.
A person of no less significance in government bureaucracy than the director of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation said not long ago that the major cause of high housing prices is unconscionable land profits. Canadians want an end to unconscionable land profits. They want an end to speculation in land. Not only do they want an end to speculation in land for housing purposes, they want an end to speculation in arable land suitable for agricultural purposes, particularly because of what has resulted in virtually every province, namely, the loss of arable land.
The people of Canada want a national land policy, the purpose of which is to provide land in appropriate areas for housing, and to preserve the land that is rich for agricultural purposes. We are getting neither of these results from the government's policies. Our people want federal policies which will protect land from all kinds of speculation, both for housing and agricultural purposes.
I have listed this afternoon some real problems for which there are immediately available honest and direct courses of action. The solutions 1 have suggested in respect of those problems are ones that do not require magic. Nor do they require a commitment from politicians that once these solutions are brought forward all the problems will disappear. In terms of the solutions I have proposed, these are things that will work and will bring a degree of decency to the lives of ordinary people. These are precisely the kinds of detailed proposals that have been absent from the government's policies, absent from the throne speech, and totally absent in the opportunism of the Official Opposition.
Before I conclude my remarks I want to say that many of the positive proposals I have made today would, I believe, make our country a more just and equitable place in which to live. Coincidentally, my party also believes that many of these policies would do more to fight inflation than that unfair, unworkable controls program the Prime Minister inflicted upon us last Thanksgiving day.
The government's controls program has been effective only in restricting the wages of working Canadians. Once again the government has not stressed the situation in respect of the unorganized working Canadians.
I was amused to note that the Prime Minister when he was in New Brunswick, when he undid his shirt, loosened his tie and once again spoke directly to the working people-and we will all recall the statement if we were watching television or were there in person, as I remember it vividly-saying that the big unions have not liked the controls program and the corporations have not liked the program but that the government brought it in for ordinary Canadians. What the Prime Minister did not include in his remarks-at least they were not recorded, and perhaps he will correct me if he did-was that

I say that the government is guilty of legalized frauds against thousands of unemployed who did indeed pay their unemployment insurance premiums because the government even ordered them taken off their gross salaries.
After that monumental blow the minister will tell the papers that unemployment is declining when it is the payroll that was cut by the subterfuges that we all know, either the recipient losing his right to benefits for all sorts of equally insignificant reasons or still because he did not answer at the set time and date a questionnaire he often received too late because of the bad postal service or because that form did not get to the office in time at the date and time set by the civil servant, and 1 am talking here about that famous rule of four consecutive weeks without pay.
Mr. Speaker, if under that rule a recipient does not receive any payments during four weeks he automatically loses his right to all those benefits and he must again work eight weeks to regain that right. That is the most nonsensical rule that has been found to date.
There was not much willingness in the Speech from the Throne to talk about the famous Anti-Inflation Act whose sole purpose has been to freeze workers' salaries since it was never used indeed to control prices and incomes of multinationals or Crown corporations no matter what one might say. Those big companies were allowed fantastic revenues of 30, 40 and even 50 per cent without a word being said. Increases exceeding the limits set in the Anti-Inflation Act were tolerated and even authorized, even for government corporations. Take postage stamps that were just increased to 10 cents and I could name thousands of multinational companies, private companies, or Crown corporations.
The government says that inflation lost ground under its Anti-Inflation Act and people know from experience that it is because the worker is losing an increasing part of his purchasing power because of the low basic exemption. It is as a result of the low basic exemption in Canada that 75 per cent of wage increases automatically return to treasury coffers. For years the government has been urged to double at least the basic exemption which would give those who earn salaries just above the average a chance to make it uphill. But no, that famous basic exemption is still maintained. Indeed, the right hon. Prime Minister is beginning to realize it because he is considering reexamining that act. I wish it will serve for once to really freeze prices and incomes, not only salaries, and especially reduce the interests of banks which are 90 per cent responsible for inflation and financial monopolies.
We dare not mention control over bank interests and monopolies, as it has been completely removed. Yet it is a major cause of inflation but we keep our hands off this dangerous topic. Nevertheless I am convinced this government will not do anything about it in spite of the review which is about to be undertaken on the Bank Act as this government is the mere lackey of those agencies which affect the daily lives of the Canadian people.

The government intends to amend the National Transportation Act. Let us hope it will deal with passenger service so that the taxpayers who make up for the deficit of the Canadian National will be able to enjoy improved services. But I would like primarily to draw the attention of the House to an issue which is not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, namely a better farm policy. In spite of all the hardships milk producers have suffered, the government has no suggestion to present to dairy farmers who are all, without exception, on the verge of bankruptcy.
Mr. Speaker, this is the worst blow in the speech. While all milk producers were expecting the announcement of a milk policy which would correct the errors of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the subject is not even mentioned. In order to remedy the lack of commercial directions from the Minister of Agriculture, all producer quotas have been reduced, and this exactly one year after dairy farmers had been asked to make an effort to produce more.
Today the same producers are penalized because they simply listened to the department one year ago. More than this, Mr. Speaker, this government, in connivance with the provinces, paid and gave grants to have our cheese processing plants closed and to favour the production of milk powder. Today we face a surplus of milk powder whereas the few remaining private cheese processing plants do not have enough milk. Our cheese processing plants do not have enough milk. Do you see the ridicule in this situation, Mr. Speaker?
While producers who have exceeded their quota reduced by the department are being penalized, while the surplus production is being seized at the rate of $10,000, $15,000 and $20,000, our cheese makers do not have enough milk to meet the market demand! Someone might say it is not true. I would forgive him, because it is unbelievable!
During the summer holiday, 1 went to see two owners of independent cheese factories in my riding and they have assured me that while they had orders to impose a fine on surplus production and send this money to the Federation of Industrial Milk Producers, they had not enough milk to meet their sales contracts. It is unbelievable!
Indeed, it is unbelievable, but these are facts I have been able to ascertain from two independent producers, while the only cheese co-operative that has survived the powdered milk storm cannot produce more for want of foresight on the part of the responsible people in the department.
Millions of dollars have been expended for building up stocks of powdered milk while cheese production has been abandoned.
So much so that during these years a cheese factory counting three generations of owners was denied grants which had indeed been accepted in principle in Ottawa, and 1 pleaded the case myself. But after the departure of the only civil servant qualified to plead for the independent cheese producers, that producer could never get a single penny from the federal government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me pay tribute to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada and to his charming wife. I also want to congratulate them for the dignity with which they perform their duties as first couple of Canada.
1 also wish to thank the Leader of the Official Opposition for the nice words he had for our leader now in hospital. After seeing him yesterday, I can tell you that he is well for the moment. He asked me to be his spokesman in the analysis of the Speech from the Throne, and I am very proud of it.
Mr. Speaker, again and again I read the Speech from the Throne after it was delivered by the Governor General of Canada in order to detect some indications of the present government's policy. The result is a most complete obscurity. But I realized that the public servants who drafted this literary work are specialized in camouflage.
In summary, they suceeded in dealing with everything and nothing. Nevertheless, parliamentarians and the public are still expecting more precise data on the government's intentions at the beginning of this new session but every time 1 hear such a speech, I am always disappointed. I finally wonder whether it would not be more serious to simply eliminate the Speech from the Throne.
The Address-Mr. C.-A. Gauthier
I wish to congratulate the movers for their speeches and for their endeavour to give an appearance of seriousness to such a lot of hot air.
1 know that theirs was a difficult task, but someone had to make a sacrifice and therefore, scapegoats were used. I must admit that there certainly are some serious and positive aspects in this speech, even though they are greatly overshadowed by the negative aspects. The only positive points are those where the government offers to help provinces in areas within their own jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am always surprised to hear of federal-provincial agreements in areas which concern only provinces. Would it not be more logical, to preserve the autonomy of the said provinces, if they were given fiscal rights tailored to their responsibilities. I find it simply ridiculous to always tell the provinces what they must do, what they need, as if provincial administrators were not just as able as those of the federal government to see to their own business. The federal government interferes in all provincial areas by pretending to help the provinces, which results in this eternal federal-provincial disagreement which will stop only when the central government no longer plays at being the great protector and minds its own business, and to do this, of course, the federal government will have to give to the provinces the fiscal powers required for their own administration. But the government would not miss such a great opportunity for maintaining the status quo and these mixed responsibilites, which aim only at confusing even more the population, at mixing everything up, so that the people and even the members of parliament can no longer distinguish what is federal and what is provincial, and I believe that this is the aim of the present government.
In the Speech from the Throne, the government talks about the independence of the country. This is great, but it is forgetting that the country is made up of provinces and that each one must feel free and independent within its own provincial jurisdiction for the country to be one day truly independent. A society will never be independent and free if its citizens are shackled. The same is true of the provinces which are the economic prisoners of the central government. That is why, whenever the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talks about Canada's independence, the words do not sound right anywhere in Canada.
The Speech from the Throne states again that Parliament will be called upon to amend the Unemployment Isurance Act. If the government wants to increase the premiums Canadian workers have to pay, while resorting to all manners of subterfuge to give claimants as little money as possible, I state right away that I am against it. If the purpose of this new legislation is to allow the minister to establish regulations to counteract the effects of the act, I am also against it. As a matter of fact, the book which contains the regulations established since the Unemployment Insurance Act came into force is three times as big as the act itself, and the sale purpose of these regulations is to exclude as many unemployed people as possible from the list of beneficiaries.
October 13, 1976

Today they would like the cheese production to double; unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, we are sorry but it is too late. We have destroyed everything and we will have to start from scratch. All cheese factories were closed, and those responsible for that state of affairs are the ones who were wishing for a monopoly. 1 heard them: they were hoping for a monopoly in the region with no competition, and that is why we now have to import from 5 to 10 million pounds of cheese every year.
I heard those so-called co-operators cry out before their members: "Cheese factories have to disappear, we have to break down competition to achieve absolute control".
To that I replied that if competition is done away with, 50 per cent of our producing province is killed. I have always maintained that even cooperatives must learn to live with competition. It is even good for them! The Speech from the Throne confirms what I advocated some ten years ago. I quote:
Significant revisions to laws promoting competition in the marketplace will be placed before you. The Government is determined to preserve and enhance Canada's traditional policy of reliance on individual enterprise as the mainspring of economic activity.
And further on:
The more effectively competition governs the marketplace, the less necessity there will be for control of the economy by governments.
And we have proof that the contrary also is true: the less competition there is, the more governments have to intervene, to bring monopolies to heel, to control multinationals.
The logical solution? The government must encourage and support private enterprise, if it wants an active economy. I ask the government to quit talking and act. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, more than ever the time has come for action, and I trust this session will be that of private enterprise.

Order, please. A few minutes ago before the speech of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) I put in general terms the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) and seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and that is the amendment which continues to
The Address-Mr. C.-A. Gauthier be under consideration by the House. 1 did not put it in specific language at that moment because I wanted to absorb the effect of the text on the amendment and to read it as one paragraph with the amendment.
The motion that is before the House at the present time is that moved by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as follows:
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the words "the people of Canada", the following words:
"We also affirm that the failure of the government to end the wage and price control program immediately, in light of the obvious inequities of the program including the practice of limiting the wages of ordinary workers while leaving profits and prices virtually unchecked, is contrary to the expressed wishes of most Canadians".
So the text which it would be proposed be added to the address by the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) would be a composite text as follows:
We respectfully affirm to Your Excellency that the Speech from the Throne is a further example of the opportunism which has cost the present administration its credibility among the people of Canada; we also affirm that the failure of the government to end the wage and price control program immediately, in light of the obvious inequities of the program, including the practice of limiting the wages of ordinary workers while leaving profits and prices virtually unchecked, is contrary to the expressed wishes of most Canadians and that your ministers no longer enjoy the confidence of this House.
Order, please. I take it there has been some discussion and agreement in keeping with the ordinary practice that this day be kept for the leaders of each party. The leaders or their nominees having spoken, at this point it is in order that I see the clock at six o'clock. Is that agreed?
